mediaItem.focusTheme_Work: Wrongful conviction, racial and religious tension, criminal justice system issues, police misconduct, ineffective defense counsel.
mediaItem.keyStats: Carl Miller served 31 years in prison for a crime he maintains he did not commit. The case hinges on the testimony of one unreliable witness, Daryl Brown. There were Brady violations including undisclosed alternate suspects and eyewitness inconsistencies.
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of the Wrongful Conviction podcast tells the story of Carl Miller, wrongfully convicted for the 1979 murder of Rabbi David Akunab in Crown Heights, Brooklyn. The episode features Carl Miller and his attorneys, James Hanning and Carissa Cocken, discussing the racial and religious tensions in Crown Heights at the time of the crime, and the flawed investigation and trial that led to Carl's conviction.  Key issues highlighted include unreliable eyewitness testimony from Daryl Brown, inconsistencies in Brown's statements, ineffective assistance of counsel, potential Brady violations regarding alternate suspects and witness information, and the influence of community pressure on the investigation. Carl Miller spent 31 years in prison despite maintaining his innocence and is now working with his legal team to fully exonerate him, especially with new evidence emerging related to other potential perpetrators.

Racial and religious tensions in the community
organizationsInvolvedRaw: Brooklyn District Attorney's Conviction Review Unit (CRU), attorneys James Hanning and Carissa Cocken.
innocenceLawyersRaw: James Hanning and Carissa Cocken are attorneys currently representing Carl Miller, aiming for his exoneration. They are working to gather new evidence and present a motion to the court, highlighting issues with the original trial and investigation.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: Rabbi David Akunab was shot and killed in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, on October 25, 1979, while walking to Yeshiva with his prayer case. The assailant, described as a young black man, stole the prayer case and fled into an apartment building.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: The key evidence was the testimony of Daryl Brown, who claimed to have witnessed Carl Miller commit the murder and run off with the prayer case.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: Carl Miller was represented by a public defender, Mr. Weiswasser, who was described as ineffective. He did not adequately challenge the prosecution's case, and in his summation, he even appeared to discredit his own client's alibi witness and praised the lead detective.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Eyewitnesses in initial lineups did not identify Carl Miller.
Inconsistencies and shifts in Daryl Brown's testimony.
Alibi witness, Joanne Davis, consistently maintained Carl's presence in Queens at the time of the murder.

Discovery issues and potential Brady violations regarding alternate suspects (Barry Lee Jackson, Derek Peterson, Willie Easterling) and eyewitness information (Shenina Sperlin's identification in Darryl Brown's lineup, Louis Fazio's doubts).

New evidence emerging in 2023, including a confession from Linda Simms implicating herself and Robert Simms in the crime and suggesting Robert Simms' potential involvement and connection to Daryl Brown.
Parole granted in 2010 after parole board considered evidence that original eyewitnesses did not identify Carl.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Potentially Linda and Robert Simms. Linda Simms confessed to her sister in 2023, implicating herself and Robert Simms in the Rabbi's murder. Robert Simms was a friend of Daryl Brown and had a motive to rob someone with a prayer bag. Robert Simms also has a history of violent crime, including a murder acquittal in a later case.

keyQuotesRaw: Carl Miller: "He didn't really do anything in defense of me. He really didn't. And a jury of 11 whites in one black. It was over 200 hesitics inside and outside the court. The deck was stacked against me."
James Hanning on trial counsel's summation: "It's a complete abdication of his duty to his client."
Carissa Cocken on Carl's parole despite maintaining innocence: "Anyone who's familiar with the criminal justice process knows that is huge."
James Hanning's call to Detective Louis Scarssella for information: "Mr. Scarssella, my phone is on. Information is information. We don't know how you factored into this."
systemicIssuesRaw: Racial and religious bias in the justice system.
Police tunnel vision and coercion of witnesses.
Issues with polygraph tests being used for coercion.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Call for anyone with information about the case to come forward.
Implicit call for justice and exoneration for Carl Miller.
Highlight the need for conviction review units to reinvestigate cases.
Suggests a need for greater scrutiny of police investigation tactics and prosecutorial conduct in wrongful conviction cases.
personalNarrativeRaw: Carl Miller describes the devastating impact of wrongful conviction, including missing out on his children's childhoods and spending 31 years of his life in prison for a crime he did not commit. He expresses the ongoing struggle to prove his innocence and rebuild his life after release.
